Analysis
text:
Method
Direct radiation is attenuated by the LiDAR-derived shading fraction per month and hour, then combined with isotropic diffuse and ground-reflected radiation on the tilted plane. Cell temperature derating follows the NOCT model; panel area and efficiency defaults are 1.6 m² and 15.3%. Surfaces without a user-specified aspect or slope take their values from the DSM terrain derivatives at the surface point.

title: Solar Potential Assessment — Bunbury
text:
This report presents a rooftop solar potential assessment for the Bunbury site (53.114°N, −2.646°E), covering the period 2020-01-01 to 2025-12-31. Seven distinct roof surfaces have been identified and characterised.
Solar irradiance estimates are derived from pre-processed ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis data, with shading calculated from Environment Agency LiDAR digital surface models. Where structures such as outbuildings or sheds sit above ground level, the DSM is adjusted upward to reflect their true rooftop height before shading is computed.

title: Solar Potential Assessment — Bunbury
text:
3 Method

3.1 Meteorological data
Hourly surface solar irradiance (global horizontal, direct normal, and diffuse horizontal components) is sourced from the ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis archive via the ecmwfr package. Data are downloaded for a 40 m buffer domain around the site centroid and aggregated to daily totals. ERA5 has a native spatial resolution of ~31 km; point-level estimates are extracted by bilinear interpolation to the site coordinates.
Plane-of-array irradiance for each surface is computed from the horizontal components using the surface tilt and azimuth, accounting for direct beam projection, isotropic diffuse sky, and ground-reflected components. Where aspect and slope are not recorded in the system parameters, values are taken from the LiDAR-derived rasters described below.


3.2 LiDAR digital surface model and shading
A 1 m resolution Digital Surface Model (DSM) is retrieved from the Environment Agency National LiDAR Programme (via nexurbr::get_gb_lidar()), covering the local domain. The DSM represents the top surface of all features — buildings, vegetation, and ground — in metres above Ordnance Datum (OSGB36/EPSG:27700).
Slope and aspect rasters are derived from the DSM using an 8-neighbour algorithm (terra::terrain()). Monthly shading fractions are then calculated using nexurbr::calc_shade(), which casts solar position vectors (sun azimuth and elevation at sub-hourly resolution) across the DSM to identify shadowed cells for each timestep.


3.3 DSM adjustment for above-ground structures
Two roof surfaces (6 and 7) are located on structures with a recorded height above the surrounding ground plane (3 m). Where height values are provided in the system parameters, the DSM cell values at those locations are raised by the stated height before shading is computed. This ensures that the shading model correctly represents the elevated surface and that neighbouring obstructions are assessed relative to the true panel position rather than the ground.
The adjustment is applied to a 1 m buffer polygon around the centroid of each elevated surface, rasterised to the DSM grid.


3.4 Yield calculation
Panel-level yield (kWh/panel/day) is computed using nexurbr::calc_solar_potential_point(), combining plane-of-array irradiance with a standard system efficiency assumption. Bank-level yield is the product of per-panel yield and panel count. Results are aggregated to monthly and annual totals for reporting.

title: Solar Potential Assessment — Bunbury
text:
6 Discussion
The analysis draws on six years of ERA5 meteorological data (2020–2025), providing a representative picture of inter-annual variability driven by cloud cover and solar geometry at this latitude (~53°N). Yield estimates are sensitive to assumed panel efficiency and inverter losses, which use standard defaults in this version of the model; site-specific values can be substituted in https://blaisekelly.github.io/GBsolar/app.html.
Shading from neighbouring vegetation and structures is captured in the LiDAR DSM but is subject to the resolution of the 1 m dataset and the date of the survey flight. Seasonal variation in deciduous canopy is not accounted for, which may lead to a modest underestimate of summer yield for surfaces adjacent to trees.
The DSM elevation adjustment for surfaces 6 and 7 (shed roof, +3 m) has a material effect on shading calculations for those surfaces; without it, the model would underestimate exposure by treating panels as if at ground level. ```
